**Solution 1 (answer 0) is wrong.** Its counting argument gives only a lower bound, g(n) = Ω(n^{2/3}). The limit needs an upper bound g(n) = o(n), which it never supplies. The conclusion is also false: the 3-AP hypergraph of a weak Sidon set has at most n−2 edges, so its average degree is at most 3. A sparse 3-uniform hypergraph has independence number Ω(n), so h(A) ≥ cn for every weak Sidon A.

**Solution 3 (answer 2/3) is wrong.** Its construction (clusters of 3-APs) does give h(A) = 2n/3. However, the Fibonacci-type set {0,1,2,4,7,12,20,33,…} is weak Sidon. I checked the pairwise sums for x<y up to 33 and found no collisions. Its 3-APs are the index triples (j, j+2, j+3) in the Fibonacci identity 2F_k = F_{k+1} + F_{k−2}. The periodic pattern 11100 (repeated) avoids every such triple, so this set has a 3-AP-free subset of density 3/5. That gives an upper bound of about 3n/5 for h, which is below 2/3. The lower-bound step ("τ ≤ n/3") is also unjustified.

**Solution 2 (answer 3/5) is the only one consistent with the checks I could make.** Its Fibonacci-based upper bound h ≤ 3n/5 + O(1) holds, and I verified the small case n = 5 (max AP-free subset of size 3). Its lower bound is asserted rather than proved (the claimed maximum degree of 3 and the "careful analysis" are not shown). So I cannot confirm that 3/5 is exact. I also cannot rule out a smaller value, since the true infimum is only known to lie in (0, 3/5]. Among the three, though, it is the most plausible.

CHOICE: 2
